prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision measurement of time

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks satisfy the criteria I apply: an original invention (Katori's magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms), an unambiguous experimental realization, independent verification by several laboratories at the 1e-18 level, and a door opened onto phenomena nobody could measure before, such as relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and many-body clock physics. Attribution is unusually clean, since five of eight colleagues name exactly Katori and Ye and no one proposes a different set. It is also a measurement tool that changes what can be seen, which is the kind of prize I find most persuasive. I have moved it up from my fifth place after reading the broad opening support and the maturity arguments. My own first choice, B001, remains a serious candidate, but I should not let it drive the committee's preferred outcome given my field.
statement.case_against: The main reservation is novelty relative to earlier prizes. The 2005 and 2012 prizes already honoured the frequency comb and the control of single trapped ions, so a clock prize risks looking like a continuation of one lineage. It is also fair to ask whether Takamoto, Ludlow, Lemonde and others who made specific milestone demonstrations are being passed over by a two-person credit. Neither point seems decisive to me, because the lattice-clock concept and its record-accuracy realizations are distinct from those earlier achievements, but the historical record of the first Sr lattice clock demonstrations should be checked carefully before we are 'absolutely sure' about who did the original work.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks are the clearest case of a new measurement technique, with an original idea, an unambiguous demonstration and broad impact, and a two-person prize is clean.
responses.response: I agree with the logic and it matches my own criteria for an original experiment that opens a door. Where I would qualify your statement is on attribution. You say Katori demonstrated the first Sr lattice clock and Ye drove record accuracy, which is a division of labour I accept, but Lemonde, Ovsiannikov and Takamoto are not resolved by the supplied credit. I would like the citation to be worded around the invention and realization of the clock, not around accuracy records, so that it rests on the original work and not on a later, more precise one.

responses.point: The decisive invention and its first realization are covered by Katori and Ye, with Hinkley, Ludlow and Lemonde important only for specific milestones, and the timing is good given independent clocks in Sr, Yb and Hg.
responses.response: This is the strongest maturity argument on the table, and I give it more weight than I did in my opening ranking. I would press one point of disagreement. You put B014 in second place, but I find its attribution harder than for the clocks: four credited names for a three-person limit, and a contested split between the theory (Jaksch, Zoller) and the experiment (Greiner, Bloch, Esslinger). That makes it less ready to be settled this year than B024, and I would keep it behind both the clocks and the moire candidate.

responses.point: Aberration correction is a clear instrumentation invention that is fully mature and widely deployed, but the 1986 prize for the electron microscope and the limited novelty in fundamental physics are reasons for caution, and Krivanek's STEM work is a possible credit issue.
responses.response: Thank you for stating the strongest case against my own first choice so fairly. I accept the Krivanek issue as real: the TEM corrector (Rose, Haider, Urban) and the STEM corrector (Krivanek and collaborators) were separate and original, and a three-name prize cannot cover both. I would resist the claim that there is little fundamental physics to recognise, since resolving atoms and interfaces directly underlies quantitative materials physics. But because only three of us ranked it and I come from this field, I treat my enthusiasm as a reason to be cautious and have moved it to an alternative.

responses.point: The Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction and the experimental discovery of correlated states at the magic angle created moire quantum matter, but the field is young and the credited set might be better limited to the two senior figures, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero.
responses.response: I share your concern about maturity, since the origin of the superconductivity is still debated, and I agree that this weighs against an early prize. I disagree on dropping Bistritzer, though. He is first author of the 2011 prediction, and removing him in order to fit a pair would sacrifice the historical record for convenience. If the committee returns to B003, I would keep all three credited names. The unresolved credit for Cao and the junior experimentalists is a further reason I would wait a few years, so I keep B003 as an alternative and not as my preferred prize.

responses.point: IceCube opened neutrino astronomy and is a major detector achievement, but the large collaboration and the AMANDA-era contributors make a three-person credit contested, and Halzen and Karle are the central names.
responses.response: I ranked B035 last, and I want to say why. I do not doubt the discovery of the diffuse flux, but the criterion is that we identify the people who did the original work, and for a collaboration of hundreds that is hard to do with three names. Your proposal of Halzen and Karle alone drops Spiering and does not remove the AMANDA and DUMAND lineage questions. I think it is the weakest candidate on attribution, though I would welcome hearing how you would justify excluding Spiering.

uncertainties: Whether the first demonstrations of the Sr lattice clock and the contributions of Takamoto, Ludlow, Lemonde and Ovsiannikov are adequately covered by crediting only Katori and Ye.
Whether a clock prize would be seen as overlapping with the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes rather than as a distinct invention.
Whether the TEM and STEM aberration-correction contributions (Rose, Haider, Urban versus Krivanek) can be fairly credited within a three-person limit.
Whether the origin of superconductivity in magic-angle graphene will be clarified soon enough that B003 is mature in another year or two.
statement.conflict_note: My profile shows a professional connection to the field of B001: I am an electron microscopist who works with aberration-corrected instruments, and I ranked it first. I have no recorded personal or institutional tie to Rose, Urban or Haider, but I flag this proximity to the field as a possible reason for recusal on B001 and have therefore not made it my preferred prize. I have no specific conflict regarding B024, B003 or the other candidates. My colleague Göran Johansson is at Chalmers Physics, but that does not bear on the candidates I am proposing.
